content: ARTS-1, also referred to as endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 1 (ERAP1), is a protein encoded by the ARTS-1 gene in humans. This protein is an aminopeptidase, an enzyme that cleaves proteins into smaller fragments known as peptides. It is primarily active within the endoplasmic reticulum, a cellular organelle responsible for protein processing and transport. The protein is known by several alternative names, including: ER aminopeptidase 1 (ERAP1), the official name recognized by the Hugo Gene Nomenclature Committee. ER aminopeptidase associated with antigen processing (ERAAP). Adipocyte-derived leucine aminopeptidase (ALAP). Puromycin-insensitive leucine aminopeptidase (PILS-AP). Functions of ERAP1: 1. Cytokine Receptor Cleavage: ERAP1 cleaves cytokine receptors located on the surface of cells. This cleavage reduces the ability of these receptors to transmit chemical signals into the cell, thereby modulating inflammatory processes. 2. Peptide Trimming for Antigen Presentation: Within the endoplasmic reticulum, ERAP1 trims peptides to prepare them for loading onto major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules. These peptides are then transported to the cell surface, where they are displayed to the immune system. If the immune system identifies these peptides as foreign (e.g., derived from viruses or bacteria), it initiates a response that leads to the destruction of the infected cell. ARTS-1 belongs to the M1 family of zinc metallopeptidases and functions as an aminopeptidase that degrades oligopeptides by sequentially cleaving them from the amino terminus. One of its critical roles is the degradation of potentially toxic peptides within the cytosol. ARTS-1 is a transmembrane protein localized to the endoplasmic reticulum and is involved in: The shedding of various cytokine receptors and decoy receptors. The trimming of antigenic peptides, which influences antigen presentation to cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Clinical Significance: Mutations in the ARTS-1 gene have been associated with an increased risk of ankylosing spondylitis, but this association is observed only in patients who are positive for the HLA-B27 allele. The protein encoded by ARTS-1 is essential for trimming precursor peptides that bind to HLA class I molecules, facilitating their presentation on MHC class I complexes. This protein can function either as a monomer or as a heterodimer in conjunction with ERAP2. Three transcript variants of the ARTS-1 gene have been identified, encoding two distinct isoforms of the protein.
